Badoo.finding: Badoo is a London-headquartered, dating-focused social network and app founded in 2006 by Russian entrepreneur Andrey Andreev (real name Andrey Ogandzhanyants). By 2013 it was among the world's most widely used dating services, operating on a freemium model, with early Russian backing from Finam. For a Russian reader around 2013 it connoted a mass-market online dating/hookup platform, not a general social network like VKontakte — a distinction the sentence's logic relies on.
Badoo.rationale: In English the brand is recognizable and no gloss is needed; in Chinese and Japanese, where the name is far less familiar, a brief descriptor (约会网站 / 出会い系サイト) is prepended to preserve the denotation that it is a dating site, at the cost of a strictly bare-name register.

DST Deal.finding: The 'DST deal' refers to the signature deal structure of Yuri Milner's Digital Sky Technologies / DST Global, made famous by the 2009 Facebook investment: large late-stage stakes at eye-catching valuations, without demanding a board seat or control, and often with Milner voting his shares with the founder. For a Russian reader around 2013 it connoted Milner's legendary, founder-friendly money — a near-mythical venture-capital model that let founders like Zuckerberg and Durov take capital without ceding power. It functioned as industry jargon with admiring, legend-tinged overtones rather than a fixed legal term.

rendering.zh: DST式交易（高估值、不要董事会席位、不干预创始人的投资模式）
rendering.ja: DST式ディール（創業者に友好的で、取締役会の席を求めない出資モデル）

DST Deal.rationale: All three renderings preserve the denotation (Milner's no-board-seat, founder-friendly model) by making the acronym adjectival ('DST-style / DST式'), sacrificing the compact insider-jargon ring of the English original; zh and ja add a brief inline gloss because Chinese and Japanese readers cannot be assumed to know DST, while English business readers get the lighter 'DST-style deal' which tech-press usage already supports.

Facebook.finding: Facebook here is the American social network launched in 2004 by Mark Zuckerberg, which by 2006 was the fastest-growing student site in the world and whose interface — narrow left sidebar, blue header, news feed, and small unobtrusive text/image ads stacked at the bottom of the left column — was reproduced almost element-for-element in VKontakte's 2006 design. Russian Wikipedia and the VK article frame VK as launched by Durov in 2006 as a Russian analogue of Facebook; in Russian press of 2006–2013 'Facebook' was used without translation as the benchmark for 'a proper Western social network', and for a 2013 reader the name evoked both a design template and the Western competitor VK was outperforming at home. The reference is period-specific: it is the mid-2000s Facebook layout, not today's Meta platform, but the proper name itself is stable across all three target languages and none of them translates it (zh keeps the Latin 'Facebook', with 脸书/面簿 only as informal or regional variants; ja uses フェイスブック in katakana glosses but Latin 'Facebook' in business writing).
Facebook.rationale: All three keep the untranslated brand name, preserving denotation and the 2013 connotation of 'Western benchmark'; the Japanese edition adds a one-time katakana gloss フェイスブック for business-biography register, and the period-specificity of the layout is left to the surrounding sentence about left-column ads rather than folded into the name. What is given up is nothing at the name level, but readers in zh and ja lose the resonance Facebook had for a Russian 2006 audience, since neither market experienced VK/Facebook as rivals.

Forbes.finding: In the context of Nikolay Kononov's 2013 book 'The Durov Code' (and the Russian tech/media landscape of the late 2000s and early 2010s), references to 'Forbes' primarily denote 'Forbes Russia' (published by Axel Springer Russia), where Kononov served as senior editor. In Russia, Forbes was the foremost publication for investigative business reporting and wealth rankings, and its Russian edition played a central role in reporting on Durov, DST, and VKontakte's cap table. While Russian texts often refer to it simply as 'Forbes', foreign readers naturally assume the global US publication unless the local edition is made explicit where context requires.
Forbes.rationale: Preserves the precise institutional reality (Kononov's own newsroom and the specific reporting entity that covered Durov) while sacrificing the Russian source text's casual shorthand, which relied on domestic readers taking the Russian edition for granted.

Game Insight.finding: Game Insight is a free-to-play social and mobile games studio founded in Moscow in 2009 (Paradise Island, Airport City, Mystery Manor, The Tribez) and still headquartered there in 2013; it later moved to Vilnius. For a Russian reader of a Durov/VK biography it named a well-known post–Mail.Ru games company associated with founders from that orbit (Chumachenko/Matsanyuk), not a foreign brand that needed explaining.
Game Insight.rationale: Kept the Latin brand as-is in all three languages (denotation and register of a proper trade name). Gave up a Chinese or Japanese phonetic transcription because the 2013 source and later coverage treat it as an untranslated English-language company name.

ICQ.finding: ICQ (from 'I seek you') was the instant messenger launched by Israel's Mirabilis in 1996, bought by AOL in 1998 and by Mail.Ru Group in 2010. In Russia and the CIS it was THE instant messenger of the late 1990s–2000s: peak of over 100 million accounts worldwide around 2001, and still 6.7 million monthly Russian users as of September 2013. A Russian reader of a 2013 Durov biography instantly recognizes it as the pre-VKontakte default of online life — the service VK itself supplanted (Mail.Ru/VK even owned it). Culturally it is the analogue of AIM for Americans, MSN Messenger for Europeans, and QQ for Chinese readers — QQ's very name (originally OICQ) derives from ICQ.

rendering.en: ICQ (the instant messenger that dominated Russian online life through the 2000s)
rendering.zh: ICQ（2000年代风靡俄罗斯的即时通讯软件，QQ的原型）
rendering.ja: ICQ（2000年代ロシアで主流だったインスタントメッセンジャー）

ICQ.rationale: All three audiences already know the bare name 'ICQ' as a technical term, but only the Russian reader carries its cultural weight, so a brief in-text apposition restores the connotation (dominant IM of the era, QQ's ancestor for Chinese readers) without resorting to a footnote. Denotation, connotation and neutral register are all preserved; the word-for-word brevity of the original is the only sacrifice.

Livejournal.finding: LiveJournal (rendered ЖЖ, 'Живой Журнал' in Russian slang) was the dominant blogging platform among Russian internet users in the 2000s, known for its one-way 'friend' follow model that VKontakte's own subscription/follower mechanism echoed. For a Russian reader in 2013, mentioning LiveJournal evokes the pre-VK blogging era and the specific asymmetric-follow UX pattern, not just a generic blog brand.

rendering.zh: LiveJournal（早期俄语博客平台，类似人人网前身的关注模式）

Livejournal.rationale: Kept the English brand name as denotation across all three since it is a proper product name; for zh added a brief functional gloss to carry the 2000s Russian blogging connotation an English reader gets for free, sacrificing brevity; ja keeps katakana with the Latin name in parentheses for business-register clarity.

Mail.ru.finding: Mail.ru began as a Russian email service and developed into a Yahoo!-like portal offering news, search, social networking and other services. By 2013 it was both an exceptionally familiar mass-market Runet brand—its email service ranked sixth worldwide—and, in context, could also stand loosely for Mail.ru Group, the major Russian internet company that had borne that corporate name since 2010. The exact denotation therefore depends on whether the passage concerns the mail service, the portal or the corporate owner.
Mail.ru.rationale: The fixed brand spelling preserves denotation and the neutral business-biography register in all three languages. It gives up the Russian reader’s immediate Yahoo!-like association and the service/portal/company ambiguity, which should be clarified by contextual wording rather than built into the name.

Mail.ru Group.finding: Mail.ru Group was the corporate name (from September 2010 until October 2021, when it was renamed VK Company Limited) of the holding company built on Yuri Milner's Russian internet assets. It was the parent of the Mail.ru email/portal service, owned the social networks Odnoklassniki and Moi Mir, and held a controlling stake in VKontakte (the report's subject), as well as stakes in Facebook and game studios. For a Russian reader around 2013 it was the dominant domestic internet conglomerate and a key shareholder in the Durov/VKontakte story, immediately recognisable by its Latin-script brand with the .ru suffix. The brand is consistently left in Latin script across en/zh/ja sources, with only the local word for 'group' translated.
Mail.ru Group.rationale: All three keep the Latin brand 'Mail.ru' (denotation and brand recognition) and translate only 'Group' into the target language; this preserves the proper-name meaning and business register while giving up nothing of substance, since the descriptive reading ('mail dot ru group') is exactly the unwanted literal gloss the source itself does not invite.

MoiFacultet.finding: MoiFacultet (Russian «МойФакультет», moifacultet.ru) was a Russian social network for university students launched in 2006, one of the direct competitors of VKontakte in its first year, mentioned in accounts of VKontakte's early history as a rival campus-network site. It never achieved significant scale and is long defunct, which is why it has no Wikipedia article and appears only in press histories of Durov. For a Russian reader in 2013 the name read as a self-evident compound 'My Faculty' (my department), evoking the student-directory niche VKontakte originally occupied. As a brand name it was written as one camel-case Latin word, like other runet startups of the era.
MoiFacultet.rationale: Preserved denotation and the startup-brand register by keeping the original Latin brand spelling, which is how runet companies of that era styled themselves; a literal translation ('My Faculty') would lose the proper-name status. Sacrificed immediate transparency of the name's meaning, recovered economically in zh and ja by a one-time parenthetical gloss rather than a footnote.

moifakultet.finding: MoiFakultet (moifakultet.ru, literally «Мой факультет», 'My Faculty') was a real Russian student-and-graduate social network launched around 2006, one of the small campus-network cohort (alongside Studlist and others) that VKontakte overtook after its October 2006 launch; the Wayback Machine shows the domain active from November 2006. For a Russian reader of 2013 the name reads instantly as a playful Russian-words brand ('my faculty/department'), signaling the university-crowd niche VK came out of. It has no standalone Wikipedia article and survives mainly in retrospective accounts of VKontakte's early competitors. It is a proper brand name, not slang, but its meaning ('my faculty') is transparent and slightly folksy to Russians.

rendering.ja: moifakultet（モイファクルチェット、『私の学部』の意）

moifakultet.rationale: Denotation (the specific defunct competitor site) is preserved by keeping the romanized brand exactly as the book does, guaranteeing consistency with 'moifakultet.ru' later; the transparent meaning is given once as a parenthetical gloss so non-Russian readers catch the campus connotation. Sacrificed: the effortless Russian-wordplay feel, which no target-language rendering can carry without renaming the brand (an unacceptable 'MyFaculty' invention).

MoiFakultet.ru.finding: No article on MoiFakultet.ru was found in Russian, English, Chinese, or Japanese Wikipedia, and general web search returned no reliable description, so I can only state what is certain from the term itself: it is a Latin-alphabet domain spelling out the Russian phrase 'мой факультет' ('my faculty/department'), and the provided gloss describes it as a short-lived Russian student social-network clone associated with the pre-VKontakte student-internet milieu around Pavel Durov. In Russian around 2013 the name would have read as a transparent, slightly playful campus-brand pun, not as an opaque proper noun; for a foreign reader the important fact is that it was a minor early Russian student social-network project, not a major or lasting platform. I cannot independently verify its exact launch date, scope, or relation to Durov's other student projects from the sources available here.

rendering.en: MoiFakultet.ru (a short-lived Russian student social network, literally 'My Faculty')
rendering.zh: MoiFakultet.ru（俄罗斯早期学生社交网络，意为“我的院系”）
rendering.ja: MoiFakultet.ru（ロシアの短期間存在した学生向けソーシャルネットワーク。「私の学部」の意）

MoiFakultet.ru.rationale: The renderings preserve denotation by keeping the original Latin brand name and supplying the transparent meaning and functional category; they sacrifice the casual campus pun because a full pun transfer is impossible without distorting a biographical register.

Motivi.finding: Motivi is a popular Italian fast-fashion/contemporary womenswear brand launched in 1993 by the Miroglio fashion group. During the late 2000s and early 2010s in Russia, Motivi operated dozens of retail boutiques in shopping malls across Moscow, Saint Petersburg, and regional capitals, functioning as an accessible European mass-market brand that sponsored beauty contests, college pageants, and media events.
Motivi.rationale: Preserves the international commercial brand identity in Latin script across English and Chinese (where foreign fashion trademarks are standardly retained in Latin alphabet without translation), while providing Japanese readers with a ruby/katakana phonetic aid for readability in business prose.

Porn King.finding: Around 2012–2013 Pavel Durov used the Latin-script Twitter name/handle Porn King as a self-conscious, English-language provocation, not as a job title in the adult industry. For a Russian reader of a reported VK biography it marked imported libertine swagger and trolling of respectability; the words were left in English in Russian media because the joke is the English itself. It is a nickname/username, not a third-party epithet like «король порно».
Porn King.rationale: Keep the Latin username so the handle remains searchable and the 2013 pose intact; add a brief gloss in zh/ja so the provocation is not opaque. Sacrifices a fully localized nickname that would look like a different person.

Ritz.finding: The most plausible referent is the Ritz-Carlton Moscow on Tverskaya 3, a five-star luxury hotel steps from Red Square, whose rooftop bar (O2 Lounge) was one of Moscow's most expensive watering holes; a Russian reader in 2013 would read 'Ritz' as shorthand for gilded-Moscow elite glitz — overpriced cocktails, expats and well-heeled foreigners rather than startup culture. The detail about elderly Americans occupying it works as an ironic tonal beat: the venue that symbolizes moneyed Moscow is actually frequented by aging Westerners, undercutting any glamour. No source ties it to a US tech conference; the Moscow reading fits a reported Durov/VK biography set largely in Russia.

rendering.ja: リッツ・カールトンのバー

Ritz.rationale: I preserve denotation (a specific, famously pricey Moscow hotel bar) and the ironic register, dropping the bare familiar 'Ritz' shorthand that only works for a Russian reader; naming the Ritz-Carlton explicitly in each language keeps the gilded-Moscow connotation legible, and zh gets the full brand name 丽思卡尔顿 as Chinese readers know the chain.

spbgu.org.finding: spbgu.org (closely linked with spbgu.ru) was an unofficial student community portal and forum for Saint Petersburg State University (SPbGU), created by Pavel Durov during his university years. It served as Durov's key playground for testing community building, user moderation, forum architecture, and early social features that directly paved the way for VKontakte in 2006.
spbgu.org.rationale: Preserves the exact literal internet domain name verbatim across all three target languages, as web addresses in biographical tech reporting function as proper historical artifacts rather than translatable prose.

Spotify.finding: Spotify is a Swedish legal music streaming service launched in 2008, positioned as a licensed alternative to piracy; by 2013 it was known in Russia mainly by reputation since it had not yet officially launched there, symbolizing the legitimate Western streaming model contrasted with piracy-driven services like VKontakte's audio section. The brand name is used identically across languages with no localized transliteration or CJK adaptation.
Spotify.rationale: Preserves denotation and brand recognition exactly as in the source; no connotation shift needed since the name functions identically as a proper noun in all target audiences, sacrificing nothing but requiring no localization since no official CJK branding existed in 2013.

«Седьмое небо».finding: Wikipedia's article on Pavel Durov confirms he studied at the Faculty of Philology of SPbSU (2002–2006) but does not mention the nickname «Седьмое небо» directly. No Wikipedia article was found explaining the term in the context of SPbSU. Based on the gloss provided (student nickname for the top-floor attic hallway at the Philology Faculty building) and the well-known Russian idiom «седьмое небо» (equivalent to 'seventh heaven'), the name is a playful, affectionate student coinage for a specific campus location. The irony is deliberate: 'seventh heaven' evokes bliss, while the actual space is a modest attic corridor. The term carries the connotation of a cherished, slightly romanticized student hangout spot.
«Седьмое небо».rationale: In all three languages the established equivalent of the idiom «седьмое небо» is 'Seventh Heaven' (en), '第七天堂' (zh), and 'セブンス・ヘヴン' (ja). These preserve the denotation and the playful connotation. What is sacrificed is the specific campus-location sense: a reader unfamiliar with the biography may read it as a generic idiom or a commercial venue name. Adding a translator's note or glossary entry at first occurrence is the standard remedy, but within the text itself the rendering should remain the recognizable idiom form.

Бертовой.finding: Бертова appears to be an ordinary Russian feminine surname referring to a private individual, a female classmate of Pavel Durov; the genitive form Бертовой is used in the biography in a possessive construction meaning 'at Bertova's' (birthday party). Wikipedia has no article on her and no mention connecting her to Durov, indicating no public notability, and for a Russian reader around 2013 the name carried no special connotation beyond identifying a peer.
Бертовой.rationale: All three renderings preserve the denotation (a surname in possessive form) and the neutral register; they sacrifice the Russian feminine-surname morphology and add no explanatory gloss, which is appropriate for a passing reference to a non-public person.

«Голден Телеком».finding: Golden Telecom (Russian pronunciation 'Голден Телеком') was a major Russian telecom and internet services provider operating 1996–2010 across Russia and the CIS; it absorbed Corbina Telecom's ISP business and Cityline, and was itself acquired by VimpelCom (Beeline) in 2007/2008, ceasing as a brand around 2010. The company deliberately used an English name as its corporate identity — the Russian form is just a transliteration, not a translation — so for a 2013 reader it connoted a big, Western-branded, 2000s-era internet/telecom player, by then already absorbed into Beeline's parent. Its web portal ('РОЛ') hosted the Aport search engine, tying it to early Russian internet culture.

rendering.ja: ゴールデン・テレコム（Golden Telecom）

«Голден Телеком».rationale: The official brand was the Latin 'Golden Telecom' in all markets, so English keeps it verbatim (preserving denotation and corporate identity). Chinese and Japanese readers may not recognize the Latin brand, so a katakana transliteration (standard for foreign company names in Japanese business writing) is given, with the Latin original in parentheses for identifiability; for Chinese the Latin name plus a parenthetical gloss keeps the corporate identity while flagging that it is a Russian telecom company, sacrificing only the phonetic pun on 'Golden'.

«единичка».finding: At St. Petersburg’s Presidential Physics and Mathematics Lyceum No. 239, parallel classes in a year are numbered; «единичка» is insider slang for the «1» stream (9-1, 10-1, etc.), the flagship olympiad-oriented mathematical class that concentrates contest winners. For a 2013 Russian reader it marked the most competitive cohort inside an already elite specialized school, not a generic homeroom.
«единичка».rationale: Kept the numbered-class denotation and the elite/olympiad connotation via quotes or a short gloss; sacrificed the untranslatable school-yard diminutive «единичка» itself.

Добромыслов.finding: Добромыслов is a common Russian surname, not limited to any widely known figure; the Russian Wikipedia disambiguation page lists several historical bearers (a surgeon, a priest, a darts player) but no VKontakte employee. I could not locate any public documentation of a VKontakte employee by this name, so for a 2013 Russian reader it would have read as an ordinary, unremarkable subordinate unless the biography itself supplies more context. The denotation is simply the surname; it carries no special slang or period connotation beyond being a standard Russian family name.
Добромыслов.rationale: Preserves the exact surname denotation with standard transliterations in each target language; because the person is not publicly identifiable, no specific connotation can be carried, and register remains neutral.

Анна Дмитриевна.finding: Name+patronymic address (имя-отчество) is the standard Russian formal/respectful way to address an older person, teacher, or professional superior; used ironically here it signals mock-formality or distance in an otherwise informal exchange with Durov. No specific identifiable public figure found under this name tied to Durov's biography; it functions as a generic formal-address device rather than a proper noun of note.

rendering.zh: 安娜·德米特里耶芙娜老师(称呼)
rendering.ja: アンナ・ドミトリエヴナ先生

Анна Дмитриевна.rationale: English keeps denotation (transliterated name) but sacrifices the patronymic's formal connotation, relying on context alone; Chinese and Japanese add a respectful title (老师/先生) to partially restore the register of formal address that the patronymic conveys in Russian, at the cost of literal denotation.

«Мой круг».finding: «Мой круг» was a Russian professional social network launched in 2005 and acquired by Yandex in March 2007. By 2013 it offered profiles, professional contacts, company pages, vacancies, and links to other social platforms, making it broadly comparable to LinkedIn in the Russian internet market. Its name literally means “My Circle” but also suggested one’s circle of acquaintances and professional network; it was a neutral brand name rather than slang.

rendering.zh: 俄罗斯版领英“我的圈子”（Moi Krug）
rendering.ja: 「モイ・クルーク」（「私の人脈」の意）

«Мой круг».rationale: English retains the established Romanized brand and supplies its literal sense. Chinese prioritizes an immediate LinkedIn analogue, while Japanese preserves the brand but glosses the professionally relevant connotation as “my network,” sacrificing strict literalness.

«Мой Мир».finding: Moy Mir (Мой Мир@Mail.Ru) was Mail.ru Group's social network launched in 2007, positioned as a competitor to VKontakte and Odnoklassniki. By 2013 it was widely seen in Russia as the older, more corporate, less 'cool' alternative to VKontakte, associated with Mail.ru's mainstream mass-market internet portal rather than youth culture — a useful contrast point in a Durov biography emphasizing VK's edgier positioning.

rendering.en: Moy Mir ("My World"), Mail.ru's social network
rendering.zh: Moy Mir（“我的世界”，Mail.ru旗下社交网络）
rendering.ja: モイ・ミール（Mail.ru運営の「マイ・ワールド」）

«Мой Мир».rationale: Preserved the transliterated proper noun plus a glossed translation and explicit attribution to Mail.ru so readers unfamiliar with Russian internet history grasp it's a rival platform, sacrificing the connotative nuance of its 'uncool/corporate' image which requires more context than a gloss can carry.

Дуров-старший.finding: In Russian journalistic writing and biographies of the Durov brothers, 'Дуров-старший' refers specifically to Nikolai Durov (born 1980), the elder brother of VKontakte founder Pavel Durov (born 1984), rather than their father Valery Durov. The suffix '-старший' mirrors the formal journalistic distinction used when two siblings share prominence in the same narrative. In Russian, it succinctly distinguishes Nikolai (the reclusive technical mastermind) from Pavel ('Дуров-младший', the public-facing CEO).
Дуров-старший.rationale: Preserves the clear relative-age distinction between the two brothers and aligns with standard biographical conventions in each language, while avoiding literal patronymic/generational ambiguity that could mistakenly point to their father Valery Durov.

«ВКонтакте».finding: ВКонтакте (lit. “In Contact”) is the Russian social network Pavel Durov launched in 2006; by 2013 it was Russia’s dominant Facebook analogue and still primarily branded as VKontakte rather than the later short form VK. For a Russian reader of a 2013 reported biography the quoted name was the company and product itself, not slang. English Wikipedia treats VK as short for original VKontakte; Japanese Wikipedia uses フコンタクテ / VKontakte with 略称 VK.
«ВКонтакте».rationale: Kept the 2013 Latin brand VKontakte as denotation; added VK and a Facebook analogue cue for zh so the product is instantly placed. Sacrificed Cyrillic and Japanese katakana フコンタクテ as too opaque in a serious biography.

Дуров.finding: The surname of Pavel Valeryevich Durov (b. 1984, Leningrad), founder of VKontakte (2006) and later Telegram (2013), the subject of the biography; his older brother Nikolai Durov co-founded both projects, so in Russian text the bare surname 'Дуров' can be ambiguous but by convention refers to Pavel unless the context is technical (Nikolai is the mathematician/programmer). Around 2013 the name carried strong connotations for Russian readers: the 'Russian Zuckerberg', a young St Petersburg IT celebrity famous for paper-plane stunts and defiant posts, then in open conflict with Mail.ru's new owners and state pressure over VK. English Wikipedia and English-language press use 'Pavel Durov'/'Durov'; Japanese Wikipedia standardizes on パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ (surname ドゥーロフ); Chinese sources give 帕维尔·杜罗夫 in simplified characters (traditional 杜洛夫), with Nikolai as 尼古拉·杜罗夫.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ
Дуров.rationale: Preserves denotation and the established onomastic form each audience already knows, sacrificing nothing except the need for disambiguation: render the first mention in each segment as the full name (Pavel Durov / 帕维尔·杜罗夫 / パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ) and use the bare surname thereafter, reserving 'Nikolai Durov / 尼古拉·杜罗夫 / ニコライ・ドゥーロフ' for the brother. For Chinese, simplified 杜罗夫 (mainland usage) is chosen over the traditional 杜洛夫 of the zh-Wikipedia title, per the simplified-character brief.

Казанский собор.finding: 这里指圣彼得堡涅瓦大街上的俄罗斯东正教喀山主教座堂，而不是莫斯科的同名教堂；它正对曾为VKontakte总部的胜家公司楼（“书籍之家”）。对2013年前后的俄罗斯读者而言，它既是无需解释的圣彼得堡市中心地标，也是供奉喀山圣母像、纪念1812年战争胜利并安葬库图佐夫的国家宗教与军事纪念建筑。

rendering.zh: 圣彼得堡喀山主教座堂
rendering.ja: サンクトペテルブルクのカザン聖堂

Казанский собор.rationale: The city qualifier preserves the exact denotation and prevents confusion with Moscow, while each language uses its established local name. This slightly sacrifices the effortless local familiarity of the unqualified Russian name but retains its neutral landmark register.

ВКонтакте.finding: ВКонтакте (VKontakte, lit. 'in touch/in contact') is the Russian social network founded by Pavel Durov in 2006, which by 2013 was the dominant SNS in Russia and the Russian-speaking world, widely seen as the Russian answer to Facebook. For a 2013 Russian reader it connoted youth, Durov's freewheeling startup ethos, and everyday internet life — the default social platform, abbreviated colloquially as VK. English and Chinese editions render it as 'VKontakte'; the Japanese edition uses the katakana フコンタクテ alongside the Latin form.
ВКонтакте.rationale: As a proper noun and brand name, denotation is fully preserved by keeping the established international form in English and Chinese; Japanese uses the standard katakana フコンタクテ (as in the Japanese Wikipedia) with the Latin form at first mention for clarity in a serious business biography. The literal meaning 'in contact' and the 2013 cultural charge are sacrificed, as with any brand name, but consistency across the book is guaranteed.

Диевский.finding: В контексте это фамилия одноклассника Павла Дурова, участвовавшего вместе с Паперно в руководстве школьной игрой в вымышленное государство. Поиск в русской Википедии не выявил статьи об этом человеке, а англо-, китайско- и японоязычные поиски не обнаружили закрепившейся формы имени. Для русского читателя 2013 года фамилия была нейтральным обозначением частного лица без заметной публичной или культурной коннотации.
Диевский.rationale: All three forms preserve the surname’s denotation and neutral biographical register without implying that the classmate was a public figure. The Chinese form corrects 季耶夫斯基 to 迪耶夫斯基 because Russian Д is represented here by 迪, while some fine phonetic distinctions and the original Cyrillic spelling are necessarily lost.

Зингер.finding: The Singer House is an Art Nouveau landmark building at Nevsky Prospekt 28, built between 1902 and 1904 for the American sewing-machine company and designed by architect Pavel Suzor. The historic and current function is as the House of Books and it was the long-time home of the city's largest bookshop. English-language Wikipedia recognizes the name Singer House and Russian-language Wikipedia identifies the building by the name Дом компании Зингер and notes it has been called Дом книги since 1938. A Chinese rendering analogous to what the Chinese reader already knows is absent — Chinese Wikipedia does not appear to have an article on the landmark — so the rendering relies on the sewing-machine brand's traditional Chinese name Singer, while Japanese has no article on the landmark either and the rendering follows the established transliteration of the company name Zinger House.
Зингер.rationale: For all three languages, keeping the Singer Company brand name as anchor carries the denotation of the landmark and the 2013 connotation of the Singer Company's presence in pre-revolutionary Russia; the existing Russian name's transliteration, connotation as a landmark of Nevsky Prospekt and the neutral register of a business biography are preserved, but any nuance of the building's nickname House of Books is dropped, as it is not part of how the building is referred to in this 2013 biography context.

Гришин.finding: In a 2013 VK/Durov narrative, Гришин is Dmitry Sergeevich Grishin (b. 1978), then CEO and later board chair of Mail.ru Group (now VK), the large portal/holding that was the principal corporate counterparty and rival to VKontakte. Russian readers of business reporting would take the bare surname as that Mail.ru executive, not a generic last name. English Wikipedia already lists him as Dmitry Grishin, co-founder/former chairman and CEO of Mail.ru Group.
Гришин.rationale: Preserved denotation as the Mail.ru CEO via established surname transcriptions (Grishin / 格里申 / グリーシン) already used for this person; first mention in each language should still expand to Dmitry Grishin / 德米特里·格里申 / ドミトリー・グリーシン plus role. Sacrificed a always-on full name and title so the original’s clipped rival-exec register survives.

«Одноклассников».finding: Odnoklassniki (OK.ru) is a Russian social network launched on 26 March 2006 by Albert Popkov, owned by Mail.ru Group (now VK) since 2008, and around 2013 it was VKontakte's main domestic rival. Its name literally means 'classmates,' and its pitch — finding old schoolmates — gave it a nostalgic, slightly older-skewing, less 'cool' image among young urban users compared with VK. For a 2013 Russian reader the genitive form «Одноклассников» (after 'серверов', 'аудитории', etc.) was instantly recognizable as the brand, with the everyday noun 'classmates' as a transparent pun. The register in the biography is neutral journalistic naming of a competitor.

rendering.ja: オドノクラースニキ（「クラスメート」の意）

«Одноклассников».rationale: All three keep the brand's Latin/katakana form for recognizability while supplying the literal meaning once, so the nostalgia and the pun with the common noun survive the genitive-case camouflage; what is sacrificed is the effortless double-reading a Russian gets, since a gloss can only annotate, not reproduce, the pun.

«Одноклассники».finding: «Одноклассники» (OK.ru) is a Russian social network launched in March 2006 by Albert Popkov, built around reconnecting with former classmates and school friends; by 2013 it was the second most popular social network in Russia behind VKontakte, with a markedly older, more mainstream/regional and 'classmate nostalgia' user base than VK's youth audience. In a 2013 biography of Durov it functions as VKontakte's older, slower, less tech-savvy chief domestic rival — the two are routinely contrasted as 'the classmates site' versus 'the students site'. The name is a proper noun meaning 'Classmates' and is transliterated consistently as Odnoklassniki in all Latin-script sources; the Japanese Wikipedia and press render it アドナクラースニキ.
«Одноклассники».rationale: Preserved the denotation (a specific named social network) and, in EN/ZH, the name's literal 'classmates' sense via a brief gloss; sacrificed nothing except that ZH drops the proposal “同学网”, which collides with an unrelated existing Chinese site (tongxue.com) and would mislead. JA follows the established Japanese rendering アドナクラースニキ rather than the ad-hoc オドノクラースニキ.

Алишер Усманов.finding: Алишер Усманов (b. 1953, Chust, Uzbekistan) is an Uzbek-born Russian metals-and-telecoms oligarch, a key figure around Gazprom ( Gazprominvestholding ), owner of Kommersant, co-owner of DST/Mail.ru Group — the vehicle behind Yuri Milner's Facebook and VK stakes — and from 2008 president of the International Fencing Federation. For a Russian reader in 2013 he personified oligarchic capital with documented Kremlin proximity, so his rumored backing of a bid for VK's founder stake carried the connotation that a state-aligned tycoon was moving on Durov's company. Chinese Wikipedia renders him 阿利舍尔·奥斯曼诺夫 (though 乌斯曼诺夫 also circulates in PRC media); Japanese Wikipedia uses アリシェル・ウスマノフ; English standardizes on Alisher Usmanov.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/アリシェル・ウスマノフ

rendering.ja: アリシェル・ウスマノフ

Алишер Усманов.rationale: All three renderings keep the denotation and the formal register of a serious business biography, using each language's established Wikipedia-standard form of the name; the Kremlin-proximity connotation is left to the surrounding text (e.g. 'oligarch' gloss in English) rather than the name itself, and for zh I chose the Wikipedia-standard 奥斯曼诺夫 over the alternative 乌斯曼诺夫 for recognizability despite slight deviation from strict transliteration.

Гриз.finding: In Nikolai Kononov's 2012–2013 biography 'The Durov Code' (Код Дурова), 'Гриз' refers to Vladimir Radionovich Grizik (Владимир Радионович Гризик), the longtime and formidable head / director of the Academic Gymnasium (Академическая гимназия СПбГУ) where Pavel Durov and his brother Nikolai studied. Students and teachers referred to him by the clipped informal school nickname/truncated surname 'Гриз' (Griz).
Гриз.rationale: Preserves the direct phonetic transliteration of the school nickname/shortened surname across all target languages, maintaining consistency with how schoolyard nicknames are handled in biographical narratives.

Казанский.finding: Refers elliptically to the Kazan Cathedral (Казанский собор) on Nevsky Prospekt in St Petersburg, built 1801–1811, one of the city's most iconic landmarks and a common informal meeting-point/landmark reference for locals ('у Казанского'). Dropping 'собор' is a colloquial St Petersburg shorthand, not a reference to Kazan Station (that's in Moscow) or the city of Kazan.
Казанский.rationale: Preserved denotation (the cathedral, not the city or a station) by expanding the ellipsis explicitly in all three languages, sacrificing the casual local-shorthand register since a bare 'Kazansky' would confuse foreign readers.

Запрещенный прием.finding: In Russian it is the 2011 theatrical title of Zack Snyder’s Sucker Punch (US original). The film mixed asylum-drama framing with stylized girl-gang action; its soundtrack featured Emily Browning’s cover of Eurythmics’ Sweet Dreams. For a 2013 Russian reader the phrase named that specific movie, not a martial-arts rule or a literal “forbidden move.”
Запрещенный прием.rationale: Each language gets the title that audience already used for the same film, preserving denotation of the work and soundtrack reference. The Russian boxing-metaphor title is sacrificed; a calque would point to the wrong movie.

«Селектел».finding: Selectel is a major Russian IT infrastructure and data center provider founded in 2008 by VKontakte co-founders Vyacheslav (Slava) Mirilashvili and Lev Leviev. Originally established to meet the massive hosting and server demands of VKontakte, it quickly expanded into an independent commercial cloud and hosting giant, becoming one of Russia's leading hosting providers.
«Селектел».rationale: Selectel is the official Latin corporate brand used internationally and domestically in Russia. Preserving 'Selectel' in English and Chinese aligns with global IT industry standards, while adding katakana with the Latin original in Japanese conforms to biographical publishing conventions for non-domestic tech firms.

Влад.finding: The term refers to a person addressed informally by first name only in Nikolai Kononov's 'Код Дурова' (2012). The most plausible referent is Vlad Tsyp lukhin (Влад Цыплухин), a developer and early associate of VKontakte who later co-founded the media company Komitet (DTF, TJournal, VC.ru). In the book he appears as a companion/assistant figure in Durov's inner circle. However, the book also mentions other Vlads, and without access to the full text passage the exact identity cannot be confirmed with certainty. For a Russian reader circa 2013, 'Влад' here carried the colloquial intimacy of a first-name-only address among young tech-industry insiders, with no patronymic or surname.
Влад.rationale: Preserved the informal first-name register and denotation in all three languages; sacrificed any disambiguation (surname) because the source text itself withholds it, and adding one would exceed what the original conveys. The transliterations are standard and consistent with the renderings already proposed by other translators.

Дворцовая площадь.finding: Дворцовая площадь is the central square of St Petersburg, named after the Winter Palace (Зимний дворец) which faces it; it connects Nevsky Prospekt with Palace Bridge and holds the Alexander Column and the General Staff arch. For a Russian reader it carries strong historical resonance (Bloody Sunday, the October Revolution) and, around 2013, was also the iconic venue of state-sanctioned mass rallies and concerts — an unmistakable symbol of Petersburg itself, and of public spectacle near the Hermitage. In the Durov/VKontakte context it likely marks a Petersburg scene or public event, and the square's name must be rendered by its established local exonym, not translated word-for-word.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/宮殿広場_(サンクトペテルブルク)
Дворцовая площадь.rationale: Each language keeps its established exonym for the landmark, preserving denotation and the imperial/revolutionary connotation at the cost of literal transparency (the Chinese name literally references the Winter Palace rather than 'palace square', and Japanese uses a plain formal toponym); register of a serious biography is preserved throughout.

Дом культуры.finding: A Дом культуры (literally 'House of Culture'; the larger variant is Дворец культуры, 'Palace of Culture') is the standard Soviet and post-Soviet municipal club institution: a state-run community arts center with concert/cinema halls, dance and music studios, hobby circles and lecture rooms, often run by a trade union, factory, or city district. For a Russian reader around 2013 it connoted a slightly shabby, bureaucratic, unmistakably Soviet public building that organizations without their own premises — exactly like a newly opened experimental gymnasium — would rent space in. In the Durov biography it is not a generic 'culture house' but the specific rented facility that physically housed the school's classes, signaling improvised, makeshift beginnings.

rendering.en: the House of Culture (a Soviet-era municipal community arts center)
rendering.zh: 文化宫（苏联式市立群众文化场所）
rendering.ja: 文化会館（ソ連式の公共地域文化施設）

Дом культуры.rationale: All three renderings keep the established calque ('House of Culture' / 文化宫 / 文化会館) and add a compact gloss so an uninformed reader grasps the denotation — a state community arts center whose rooms could be rented; zh 文化宫 is especially apt because China has the identical institution, so it needs no analogue-building. Sacrificed is the full connotative weight (the drab, makeshift, post-Soviet flavor) and the Дом/Дворец size distinction, which would require a footnote rather than an inline rendering.

День города.finding: День города Санкт-Петербурга — официальный городской праздник, отмечаемый 27 мая (день основания города Петром I в 1703 году), с массовыми гуляниями, концертами, салютом. Для петербуржца это узнаваемая ежегодная городская дата, институционально закреплённая, а не абстрактный 'городской фестиваль' — упоминание в биографии Дурова, вероятно, привязывает событие к конкретному дню/сезону (конец мая) в Петербурге, где училась ВКонтакте команда.
sources: general knowledge of Russian municipal holidays

rendering.en: City Day (St. Petersburg's annual founding-day holiday)
rendering.zh: 圣彼得堡建城日（城市日）
rendering.ja: 「市の創立記念日」（サンクトペテルブルクの都市の日）

День города.rationale: Preserves denotation (a specific civic holiday tied to the city's founding) and adds a brief gloss so foreign readers grasp its institutional, calendar-specific nature, sacrificing the compactness of the Russian original.

Twitter.finding: This refers to the American microblogging and social-networking service launched in 2006, not merely to its operating company. By 2012–2013 it was a globally prominent, rapidly scaling platform—processing hundreds of millions of posts daily—and thus a recognizable example for a Russian reader of infrastructure strained by explosive growth. The service retained the name Twitter throughout the book’s historical setting; it was renamed X only in July 2023.
Twitter.rationale: These established contemporary names preserve the historical denotation and the neutral business-technical register. They deliberately avoid the anachronistic name X; the Chinese rendering sacrifices the original spelling but retains immediate recognition.

Zynga.finding: Zynga Inc. is a San Francisco-based American social-game developer and publisher founded in April 2007 and best known for FarmVille, Words with Friends and Zynga Poker on Facebook. Around 2013 it was a shorthand for the Facebook-platform social-gaming boom (and then bust — its post-2011 IPO decline was widely reported), and it appears in the Durov/VKontakte biography because VKontakte's own social games competed in the same space. Russian, English, Chinese and Japanese Wikipedias all treat it as a familiar brand name; Russian keeps the Latin 'Zynga', Chinese pairs it with 星佳 (Zynga China), and Japanese renders it ジンガ.
Zynga.rationale: The Latin brand name is preserved in all three because the audiences already know it; zh and ja add a brief gloss (星佳 for zh, katakana ジンガ for ja) so non-specialist readers get the analogue without a footnote. Denotation and connotation (social-gaming boom) are kept; nothing is sacrificed except absolute bareness, which the register does not require.
